Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a plaintiff need not plead a prima facie case of discrimination to survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, but must allege facts supporting a plausible inference of discrimination.

Cite at least six decisions of the Fourth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### I. A Title VII Plaintiff Need Not Plead a Prima Facie Case. She Must Allege Facts That Make Discrimination Plausible.

**A. The prima facie case is an evidentiary framework, not a pleading requirement.**

The Supreme Court has held that the *McDonnell Douglas* prima facie case "is an evidentiary standard, not a pleading requirement." *Swierkiewicz v. Sorema N.A.*, 534 U.S. 506, 510 (2002). The framework governs how proof is allocated at summary judgment or trial. A complaint therefore need not "contain specific facts establishing a prima facie case of discrimination." *Id.* at 508, 511–12. It need only satisfy Rule 8(a)(2)'s requirement of "a short and plain statement of the claim." *Id.* at 512. The Court added that Rule 8(a)'s simplified standard "applies to all civil actions." *Id.* at 513.

This Court has applied that rule consistently. A plaintiff "is not required to plead facts that constitute a prima facie case in order to survive a motion to dismiss." *Coleman v. Md. Court of Appeals*, 626 F.3d 187, 190 (4th Cir. 2010), *aff'd*, 566 U.S. 30 (2012). *Accord McCleary-Evans v. Md. Dep't of Transp.*, 780 F.3d 582, 584–85 (4th Cir. 2015). See also *Woods v. City of Greensboro*, 855 F.3d 639, 648 (4th Cir. 2017). *Bryant v. Aiken Regional Medical Centers Inc.*, 333 F.3d 536, 545–46 (4th Cir. 2003), reflects the same understanding of *Swierkiewicz* at the Rule 12(b)(6) stage. A district court that dismisses a discrimination complaint because it does not recite each element of a *McDonnell Douglas* prima facie case applies the wrong standard.

**B. The complaint must still allege facts that plausibly support an inference of discrimination.**

Dispensing with the prima facie case does not dispense with Rule 8. After *Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly*, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007), and *Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009), a complaint must plead "enough facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face." This Court has said that *Swierkiewicz* remains good law but "did not alter" that obligation. See *McCleary-Evans*, 780 F.3d at 584–85. Instead, a plaintiff must allege facts that satisfy the elements of the cause of action. *Goode v. Cent. Va. Legal Aid Soc'y, Inc.*, 807 F.3d 619, 626 (4th Cir. 2015); *Coleman*, 626 F.3d at 190–91. The elements of a prima facie case are a useful guide in judging whether a complaint is plausible, but they are not a checklist the plaintiff must complete. In *Woods*, 855 F.3d at 648, the Court asked whether the facts alleged, taken as true, plausibly showed that the employer acted because of a protected characteristic.

*McCleary-Evans* shows where the line falls. The plaintiff there alleged only that she was qualified, that she was rejected, and that the decisionmakers must have been biased. The Court found those allegations merely "consistent with" discrimination. They did not make it plausible, because the complaint offered no facts connecting the decision to race or sex, and it offered "obvious alternative explanation[s]." 780 F.3d at 585–86. A complaint falls short when it relies on conclusions and speculation. It does not fall short merely because it omits a particular prima facie element.

The Court evaluates a complaint under these principles by reading it as a whole. It accepts well-pleaded facts as true and draws reasonable inferences in the plaintiff's favor. Plausibility is "a context-specific task." *Francis v. Giacomelli*, 588 F.3d 186, 193 (4th Cir. 2009). The Court asks whether the facts, taken together, nudge the claim "across the line from conceivable to plausible." *Twombly*, 550 U.S. at 570. A plaintiff is not required to prove her case or to rule out lawful explanations at this stage. *See Swierkiewicz*, 534 U.S. at 511–12; *Coleman*, 626 F.3d at 190.

**C. Application.**

Plaintiff's complaint does more than assert bias. It alleges facts about her protected status, her qualifications and performance, the adverse action, and the circumstances surrounding it. Those circumstances include the treatment of comparators outside her protected class, the decisionmakers' statements or conduct, and the timing and irregularity of the decision. [Insert record-specific allegations with complaint citations.] Together, these facts support a reasonable inference that her protected status was the reason for the adverse action. That is all *Swierkiewicz*, *Coleman*, and *McCleary-Evans* require. The Court should reverse the dismissal and remand for discovery.
